messages.author: cffafe975818feab
messages.subject: Dealing with track avoidence
parts:
Hi,



I have been sampling kangaroo density along tracks, and have
used animals with GPS collars to test whether tracks are being avoided. The results
suggest kangaroos tend to be between 6-11% further form track than expected, had
distribution been completely random. This difference was significant within 50m
and 100m from track, but not at 200m.



Avoidance is not a strict non use of area near track, rather
a tendency to be further away, which makes it difficult to deal with. How
exactly can this type of avoidance me dealt with?







The only idea I had was to model the affect of avoidance as distance
from line increases, and adjust kangaroo distance (from sampling) values
accordingly. For example, kangaroos tend to be 9% further from line at 50m, 11%
at 100m and 6% at 200m, so adjustment term could be created. This approach does
not allow me to take into account tracks over the entire study region however.



The only approach I have seen applied, is to left truncate
to the point of avoidance, then remove that area of avoidance from the study
region. This is not possible here, as there is no strict no use area.






A quick side issue. I have seen left truncation applied to dealing
with reactive movement and track avoidance. My understanding is left truncation
is not justified in dealing with reactive movement. Am I right is this thought?






And yes I agree sampling along tracks is not a good idea for
numerous reasons, including the occurrence of track avoidance :)






Cheers



Brett

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with track avoidence
parts:
Hi Brett,

I would say that if you know the "true" distribution of animals with respect to
distance from the transect line from your radio data, then you can combine this
knowledge with observed distances to estimate the detection function. This
approach is detailed in Tiago Marques' PhD thesis, which is available at
http://hdl.handle.net/10023/391
see chapters 4 and 5. You can't do it in Distance, but the methods could be
programmed in R.

Regarding left truncation, it seems OK if the animals within some distance x
tend to show responsive movement and leave the area completely (so they are not
counted at all within the right truncation w). But it's not OK if they leave
the strip out to distance x but move out a bit into distances between x and w.
Then left truncation will produce a positive bias in the density estimate.

Good luck!

- Len Thomas
